"title": "Toxicity of TiO2, SiO2, ZnO, CuO, Au and Ag engineered nanoparticles on hatching and early nauplii of Artemia sp",
"authors": "Ch Lakshmi N Murthy; Mohammed M Idris; Shashi Singh",
"field_subfield": "Ecotoxicology / Nanotoxicology",

"executive_summary": "This study investigates the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles (silver, gold, copper oxide, zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, and silicon dioxide) and three soluble salts (CuSO4, ZnSO4, and AgNO3) on the hatching of Artemia sp. cysts and the viability of early nauplii. The authors highlight that nanomaterials pose risks to ecosystems due to their unique physicochemical properties, and there is a dearth of information on their bioavailability and behavior under varying conditions such as pH and salinity. Using Artemia as a cost-effective model organism, the study exposes hydrated and bleached cysts to nanoparticles in aerated, filtered sterile salt water and records hatching rates and nauplii viability. The toxicity order is estimated as Ag>CuO>ZnO>Au>TiO2>SiO2. Nanoparticles were characterized using TEM and DLS, showing reduced size in high salt concentrations and visible flocculation for copper and zinc oxide. The hatching rate dropped significantly in the presence of silver and copper oxide, with the highest effect at 100mg/L. A parallel standard Artemia toxicity test monitored nauplii viability, with mortality as the endpoint. The LC50 of silver nanoparticles was around 10.12mg/L at 24 hours, and 80% of nauplii died in silver nitrate solution within 24 hours. The study found a strong inverse correlation (coefficient of -0.7853) between hatching rates and larval mortality, suggesting that hatching can serve as a sensitive bioassay for nanoparticle toxicity. Oxidative stress was assessed using DCFDA staining, with silver nanoparticles showing the highest ROS staining. The authors conclude that Artemia is a suitable model organism for nanoparticle ecotoxicity, and the hatching test combined with the standard lethality test could be used as a pre-screening tool for nanoparticle toxicity. The study also notes that nanoparticles remain stable in seawater up to one week, though ionic or dissolved components may settle due to precipitation. The pH of salt water did not change upon nanoparticle addition, remaining around 6.3-6.5 up to 48 hours. The experiment was repeated six times, and data were analyzed using GraphPad software. The study emphasizes the importance of hazard identification in risk assessment of nanomaterials, and the advantages of the assays include being easy to perform, short-term, and using mortality as an endpoint. The authors also note that the use of cysts available in enormous quantities as batches cuts down on variability, and the assay can be adopted for high-throughput hazard identification of nanomaterials. The study does not report detailed demographic information or specific statistical tests beyond the paired T-test, and the bibliography is omitted, so top_influential_citations is set to \"\". The ethical considerations are not explicitly reported, so this field is set to \"\". The data and code availability are not explicitly reported, so this field is set to \"\". summary.title: Toxicity of TiO2, SiO2, ZnO, CuO, Au and Ag engineered nanoparticles on hatching and early nauplii of Artemia sp
summary.authors: Ch Lakshmi N Murthy; Mohammed M Idris; Shashi Singh
summary.executive_summary: This study assessed the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles (silver, gold, copper oxide, zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, and silicon dioxide) and three soluble salts (CuSO4, ZnSO4, and AgNO3) on the hatching of Artemia sp. cysts and on the viability of newly hatched nauplii. The researchers used the brine shrimp Artemia as a model organism because of its ubiquitous distribution, robust nature, and cost-effective culture, making it suitable for toxicological assays. The study employed two complementary endpoints: hatching rate of hydrated cysts and mortality of nauplii in a standard toxicity test. Nanoparticles were characterized using transmission electron microscopy and dynamic light scattering, both in distilled water and salt water, to understand their physicochemical behavior. The hatching experiments were conducted in 25% salt water at 28°C with continuous aeration and light for 24 hours, while the standard toxicity test monitored nauplii viability at intervals up to 48 hours. The results revealed a clear order of toxicity: Ag>CuO>ZnO>Au>TiO2>SiO2, with silver and copper oxide being the most toxic. The study found a strong inverse correlation (coefficient of -0.7853) between hatching rates and larval mortality, suggesting that hatching rate could serve as a viable bioassay for nanoparticle hazard assessment. The findings have implications for environmental risk assessment and the development of high-throughput toxicity screening methods for nanomaterials.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study assessed the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles (silver, gold, copper oxide, zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, and silicon dioxide) and three soluble salts (CuSO4, ZnSO4, and AgNO3) on the hatching of Artemia sp. cysts and on the viability of newly hatched nauplii. The researchers used the brine shrimp Artemia as a model organism because of its ubiquitous distribution, robust nature, and cost-effective culture, making it suitable for toxicological assays. The study employed two complementary endpoints: hatching rate of hydrated cysts and mortality of nauplii in a standard toxicity test. Nanoparticles were characterized using transmission electron microscopy and dynamic light scattering, both in distilled water and salt water, to understand their physicochemical behavior. The hatching experiments were conducted in 25% salt water at 28°C with continuous aeration and light for 24 hours, while the standard toxicity test monitored nauplii viability at intervals up to 48 hours. The results revealed a clear order of toxicity: Ag>CuO>ZnO>Au>TiO2>SiO2, with silver and copper oxide being the most toxic. The study found a strong inverse correlation (coefficient of -0.7853) between hatching rates and larval mortality, suggesting that hatching rate could serve as a viable bioassay for nanoparticle hazard assessment. The findings have implications for environmental risk assessment and the development of high-throughput toxicity screening methods for nanomaterials.

Research Context
Nanomaterials pose risks to environment and human health due to their unique properties. There is a dearth of information on the impact of nanoscale objects on the environment. The behavior of nanoparticles in various conditions like pH, salinity, and biotic factors is not clearly known. Hazard identification is an important step for risk assessment of nanomaterials. Many ecotoxicology assays have been tested for nanomaterials in bacteria, fishes, copepods, and Daphnia. Few studies have used Artemia sp. for nanomaterial toxicity, and hatching of hydrated cysts has rarely been used as an endpoint.

Research Question And Hypothesis
What is the toxicity order of the tested nanoparticles on Artemia sp. hatching and nauplii viability? Can hatching rate of hydrated cysts serve as a valid endpoint for nanoparticle toxicity assessment? Is there a correlation between hatching rates and larval mortality in nanoparticle suspensions? Can Artemia hatchability test be used as a pre-screening test for nanoparticle toxicity? The predicted outcome was that silver and copper oxide would be the most toxic nanoparticles.

Methodological Details
Six engineered nanoparticles and three soluble salts were tested on Artemia sp. Silicon nanoparticles were supplied by Nanologica AB. Silver nanoparticles were obtained from Colorobbia. Gold nanoparticles were obtained from INMETRO. Copper oxide nanoparticles were from Intrinsiq Materials (UK). Zinc oxide nanoparticles were from Nanogate (Germany). Titanium dioxide particles were synthesized in house using an existing protocol. Nanoparticles were characterized using TEM and DLS. TEM studies used JEOL 2010 TEM at 100KV with 20µ aperture. DLS measurements were conducted using Horiba Nanopartica SZ100. Artemia cysts used were the San Francisco Bay strain. Cysts were hydrated in distilled water under aeration for 45 minutes. Cysts were bleached using 20% sodium hypochlorite solution for 15 minutes. Bleached eggs were washed 6 times with distilled water. Hatching was conducted in 25% salt water at pH 8.0. Temperature was maintained at 28°C for hatching. Nanoparticles were added at concentrations of 100mg/l and 10mg/l. The experiment was repeated six times. Three aliquots of 100µl were taken from each flask. Nauplii viability was counted at intervals of 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, and 48 hours. LD50 was calculated using Graphpad software. Nauplii were exposed to concentrations of 100mg/l, 10mg/l, 1mg/l, 0.1mg/l, and 0.01mg/l. DCFDA was used at a concentration of 10µM for oxidative stress testing. Oxidative stress was imaged using Zeiss Axiovert imager. The validity criterion for hatching studies was low mortality in the control. The validity criterion for toxicity tests was mortality below 10% in 24 hr. The correlation test was performed using online software and Microsoft Excel.

Procedures And Architectures
A suspension of SiO2, TiO2, CuO, and ZnO NPs was made at 2mg/ml. The suspension was sonicated at ~30W with a pulse of 50% for 10 minutes. Silver nanoparticles were obtained as a suspension at 4% with PVP as a stabilizing agent. Gold nanoparticles were in water at a concentration of 0.006%. Working dilutions were made in salt water (NaCl). TEM studies applied a 50µg/ml suspension to formvar coated copper grids. About 10 images were taken using GATAN camera. DLS measurements were conducted at 25µg/ml in milliQ water and salt water. Each suspension was analyzed thrice for three days. Hatching was counted after 24 hours for each culture. Number of hatched Artemia (immotile vs. motile), umbrella stage, and unhatched cysts were counted. Hatching rate was expressed as percent of total number of fully hatched Artemia. Nauplii were transferred to six well plates for the toxicity test. Mortality was recorded as cessation of swimming or any movement by nauplii. Oxidative stress was observed using DCFDA which reacts with ROS. The hatching studies were conducted 6 times. Brine shrimp normally showed a hatching rate of 74%+5.5. The viability of hatched nauplii was about 97%. The pH of salt water remained around 6.3-6.5 up to 48 hours. Artemia were not fed during the test period. LC50 was calculated for each particle.

Key Results
The order of toxicity was estimated as Ag>CuO>ZnO>Au>TiO2>SiO2. The highest toxic effect was seen in silver and copper oxide nanoparticles. The hatching rate dropped to about 29% in silver and copper oxide at 100mg/L. Only 50% of hatched Artemia were motile and viable at 100mg/L. The hatching rate remained lower at 10mg/L of silver nanoparticles. The viability of hatched nauplii was good at 85% at 10mg/L of silver. In copper oxide, hatching rate was low with better viability around 64%. Hatching rate was low in gold, silicon, titanium, copper, and zinc oxide at around 50-60%. Post-hatching mortality was not very high in these nanoparticles. In zinc oxide, hatching rate was high at 60% but cysts had a tendency to clump together. In titanium dioxide at 100mg/L, hatching rate was 41.50% with 67.8% viability. In titanium dioxide at 10mg/L, hatching rate was 54% showing ~90% viability. Gold and silicon dioxide nanoparticles displayed very good viability after hatching. SiO2 nanoparticles at 10mg/L displayed hatching rate and viability equivalent to controls. Silver in ionic form was highly toxic as 80% of nauplii were dead in 24 hours. The LC50 of silver nanoparticles was around 10.12mg/L at 24 hours. The correlation coefficient between hatching rates and mortality was -0.7853. Comparing viability of nauplii with hatching rate showed no statistically significant difference (P=0.683). The standard Artemia toxicity test results were comparable. Silver nanoparticles ranked very high in toxicity, followed by copper and zinc oxide. Titanium dioxide, gold, and silicon nanoparticles showed better survival up to 48 hrs. The particles that reduced hatching rate showed an increase in mortality in the ARC test. The nauplii showed accumulation of eNPs in the gut of Artemia by end of 24 hours. In case of silver nanoparticles, dead nauplii did not show accumulation of material in the gut. Nauplii exposed to silver nanoparticles showed highest staining for ROS and superoxide. Nauplii exposed to other nanoparticles did not show signs of ROS or superoxide. Silver and copper oxide nanoparticles did not show gross morphological abnormalities. There were no changes in morphology of nauplii hatched in presence of nanoparticles. Staining of hatched Artemia with DCFDA showed staining for ROS in few still trapped nauplii and the gut of dead nauplii.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The strong inverse correlation between hatching rates and larval mortality implies hatching rate can be a bioassay. The toxicity of silver and copper oxide could be due to ionic forms. Ionic silver precipitates out due to high salinity but still affected hatching and viability. Silver nitrate and copper sulfate representing ionic forms also showed high toxicity. Silicon nanoparticles at low concentration were very conducive and showed better hatching than control. The particles that reduced hatching rate showed increased mortality in the ARC test. The nanoparticles remained stable in seawater up to one week. The ionic or dissolved component may settle down due to precipitation. Continuous aeration in the hatching test keeps the particles in suspended form. Artemia is a filter feeder and NPs may enter the guts through ingestion. The mortality observed may be due to the uptake of eNPs clogging the gut. Artemia with capacity to homeostasis in variable external salt concentrations appears to be a model organism. Suitability of Artemia for toxicity tests was established. Artemia is often used in pharmaceutical industry and for metal and radiation toxicity. The Artemia hatchability test could be used as a pre-screening test for nanoparticle toxicity. These acute toxicity tests eliminate the need of laboratory maintenance of test species. Use of cysts available in enormous quantities as batch cuts down on variability. This assay can be adopted for the hazard identification of nanomaterial and high throughput methods.

Claims
The toxicity order of the tested nanoparticles on Artemia sp. is Ag>CuO>ZnO>Au>TiO2>SiO2. The order of toxicity was estimated as Ag>CuO>ZnO>Au>TiO2>SiO2. The highest toxic effect was seen in silver and copper oxide nanoparticles. The hatching rate dropped to about 29% in silver and copper oxide at 100mg/L. Silver in ionic form was highly toxic as 80% of nauplii were dead in 24 hours. The LC50 of silver nanoparticles was around 10.12mg/L at 24 hours. Silver nanoparticles ranked very high in toxicity, followed by copper and zinc oxide. Silicon nanoparticles at low concentration were very conducive and showed better hatching than control. SiO2 nanoparticles at 10mg/L displayed hatching rate and viability equivalent to controls. The toxicity of silver and copper oxide could be due to ionic forms. The nanoparticles remained stable in seawater up to one week. The mortality observed may be due to the uptake of eNPs clogging the gut.
Hatching rate of hydrated cysts can serve as a valid endpoint for nanoparticle toxicity assessment. Both the tests show good inverse correlation in sensitivity to nanoparticles. The correlation coefficient between hatching rates and mortality was -0.7853. The particles that reduced hatching rate showed increased mortality in the ARC test. Artemia hatchability test could be used as a pre-screening test for nanoparticle toxicity. Hatching of hydrated cysts has not been used as an endpoint for toxicity except in [14]. Few studies have used Artemia sp. for nanomaterial toxicity. These acute toxicity tests eliminate the need of laboratory maintenance of test species. This assay can be adopted for the hazard identification of nanomaterial and high throughput methods. Use of cysts available in enormous quantities as batch cuts down on variability.
There is a strong inverse correlation between hatching rates and larval mortality in nanoparticle suspensions. The correlation coefficient between hatching rates and mortality was -0.7853. The particles that reduced hatching rate showed increased mortality in the ARC test. The standard Artemia toxicity test results were comparable. Our results correlate with some other toxicity assays performed on Artemia using nanoparticles. Comparing viability of nauplii with hatching rate showed no statistically significant difference (P=0.683). Hatching or emergence of the nauplii has been used as a sensitive bioassay to study the molecular and physiological effects of metals. Lower hatching rate equates with the toxicity of test compound. Artemia with capacity to homeostasis in variable external salt concentrations appears to be a model organism.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The hatching studies have been conducted 6 times. The experiment was repeated six times. Each suspension was analyzed thrice for three days. The data was represented as mean + SEM. The validity criterion for hatching studies was low mortality in the control. The validity criterion for toxicity tests was mortality below 10% in 24 hr. The pH of salt water did not change upon addition of nanoparticles. Hatched nauplii appeared normal and swimming vigorously. There were no changes in morphology of nauplii hatched in presence of nanoparticles. Silver and copper oxide nanoparticles did not show gross morphological abnormalities.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 shows the hatching rate, mortality, and viability of Artemia exposed to nanoparticles. Figure 3 shows the hatching rate of brine shrimp altered drastically in presence of nanoparticles. Figure 4 shows the hatching rate was low in presence of other nanoparticles. Figure 5 shows the accumulation of eNPs in the gut of Artemia by end of 24 hours. Figure 6 shows the strong correlation in hatching rates and larval mortality. Figure 1 shows the transmission electron microscope studies show no apparent change in aggregation or dispersion of particles. Figure 2 shows the nanoparticles exhibited different behaviour in salt water. Figure S1 shows the nanoparticles suspended both in Milli Q water and 25%NaCl solution were measured up to 48 hours. Figure S2.1-2.6 shows the nauplii had emerged but were immotile/dead; some were still-dead and trapped in the membrane. Figure S3 shows the staining of hatched Artemia with DCFDA for signs of stress. Table 2 shows the viability of nauplii to various nanoparticles.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the establishment of the toxicity order of the tested nanoparticles on Artemia sp. 2. The strongest evidence is the strong inverse correlation between hatching rates and larval mortality. 3. The future path is the use of Artemia hatchability test as a pre-screening test for nanoparticle toxicity.
